Canonical coordinates on a Lie group
The Geometry of the Euclidean Group

scenes.title: Paper-Map Globe
scenes.brief: A slate globe hovering in 3D with 4–6 translucent flat paper maps (blue) that each cover a cap. Hover any point: its dot lights up on every map that covers it. Where two maps overlap, a purple "translation arrow" shows the change-of-map function ψ∘φ⁻¹ as a warped grid; a smoothness meter stays lime (no creases, derivatives continuous). Toggle a "bad map" with a crease: the meter flashes coral. Final beat: an orange map F from the globe to a donut, read through charts as an ordinary function between two flat grids.

scenes.title: Touching Sheet
scenes.brief: A ball (blue) with a flat translucent sheet resting on it at a draggable teal point p. An orange arrow on the sheet; a gold "temperature" field painted on the ball as color; the arrow's readout is the rate the temperature changes when you walk that way (a derivation). Two basis arrows ∂/∂x₁, ∂/∂x₂ (red, green) show coordinates. A smooth map F (ball → stretched egg) carries the sheet and its arrow: the pink pushed arrow appears on the egg's sheet; composing two maps multiplies their arrow-pushers (chain rule). Finally, all sheets at all points are stacked into a hairy "bundle" view with a projection back down.

scenes.title: Covector Stacks
scenes.brief: Covectors drawn as stacks of parallel purple lines (planes in 3D) with spacing = 1/size. An orange arrow (tangent vector) is dropped on a stack: the readout counts lines crossed = ⟨ω, X⟩, linear in the arrow. dx₁, dx₂ appear as the stacks of the grid lines. A gold hill f with its contour lines: zooming in at p, the contours become a straight stack = df(p). A map F sends arrows forward (pink) while covector stacks are pulled back (purple) so that "lines crossed" matches on both sides.

scenes.title: Flows & Brackets
scenes.brief: A plane (or sphere) filled with small orange arrows of a vector field X. Drop teal leaves: they float along integral curves (computed by RK4), and the whole sheet of dots flows as Φ_t. A gold scalar field shows Xf as a colored readout of its rate along the flow. Second field Y in blue: the bracket beat runs "flow X for ε, Y for ε, X back, Y back" and the coral gap from start, divided by ε², converges to the pink arrow [X,Y]. A final panel verifies skew-symmetry and Jacobi as three arrows summing to zero.
beats: 📈 rate of change along the flow

scenes.title: Lie Group Zoo
scenes.brief: A zoo of cages, each holding a smooth group shown as a surface: a line/plane (Rⁿ, sliding), a circle (SO(2)), a ball-ish shape for SO(3) (pick a rotation by axis-angle point), SE(3) as a frame floating in space, and GL(2) as a squishing grid. In each, grab element g (orange) and h (blue); the product gh (pink) moves smoothly as you drag; inverse is a mirror ghost. A left-vs-right toggle shows L_g (move the whole picture in world coords) vs R_g (move it in body coords); a lime readout shows L_g∘R_h = R_h∘L_g.

scenes.title: Velocity at Home
scenes.brief: The identity e is a gold "home" dot on the group surface with its tangent sheet. Drag an orange arrow ξ at home; tapping "copy" left-translates it to every point so the group fills with a left-invariant field (arrows move rigidly with g). Two such fields, X_ξ and X_η, run the go-go-back-back loop; the gap at home is [ξ,η]. For SO(3): ω arrows in 3D and the hat matrix lit entry by entry; the bracket readout equals the cross product arrow ω₁×ω₂ (pink). For SE(3): two screws; the bracket's (ω, v) parts appear as arrows.

scenes.title: Keep Stepping
scenes.brief: Start at gold home e with an orange velocity ξ. Slider n: take n equal small steps (I + ξ/n)ⁿ, each drawn as a ghost frame; as n grows the ghosts merge into a smooth curve that equals exp(ξ) (lime match readout). A series panel adds Aᵏ/k! terms one by one as stacked bars converging. Spin mode: a frame turning about ω (Rodrigues, sin/cos dials). Screw mode: a frame corkscrewing along an axis (rotation + slide). Log mode: drag a pink target frame; the scene finds the ξ that reaches it and shows a second ghost path (−ω, 2π−θ) landing on the same target.

scenes.title: Exp Coordinates
scenes.brief: Two ways to give a rotation (or rigid motion) numbers. First kind: three orange sliders σ blend axes into one arrow and take a single exp — one straight path from home. Second kind: three sliders θ each spin about a fixed axis in turn — a three-segment path (like Euler angles or a robot arm's joints) reaching the same pink frame. Then a "tile" beat: the small patch of coordinates around home is copied to other places by left-shifting, covering the whole group like the paper-map globe.

scenes.title: Dance Rules
scenes.brief: A dance floor of teal points. Pick a group element g (orange knob): every point moves by the same rule Φ_g (a crowd dancing in sync). Identity leaves all still; doing h then g equals doing gh (lime check). Tracing one dancer under all g paints its orbit. Conjugation: watch a motion h from a moved viewpoint g → ghg⁻¹. Ad: a twist arrow is re-expressed in the moved frame; coadjoint: a wrench (purple) re-expressed so that pairing stays fixed. Lifted action: each dancer carries a small velocity arrow that turns along with it.

scenes.title: Body vs Space
scenes.brief: A slate fixed frame A and a blue body with frame B moving along a curve g_ab(t). Points (teal) carry a 1 in their 4th slot and translate; free arrows carry 0 and only rotate. Any start-to-end placement is reached by one screw (gold axis, pitch dial). Velocity panel: the body twist V^b drawn at B and the spatial twist V^s drawn at A's origin, linked by Ad_g (6×6 matrix tiles light up). A purple wrench and orange twist show a work readout that stays the same in every frame. Frame-change sliders show which velocity changes (coral) and which is unaffected (lime), and that chained velocities add only after Ad.

scenes.title: No Fair Ruler
scenes.brief: Two twists (orange, blue) look perpendicular (lime right-angle badge) in frame A; drag the reference frame origin and the badge turns coral as the R⁶ dot product changes. Rⁿ panel: a ruler-ellipse Ψ survives every rotation only when it is a circle (αI). SE(3) panel: a 6×6 grid of block tiles; spinning random h through Adᵀ Ψ Ad shows only the [[0,β],[β,γ]] pattern survives, and the top-left block is forced to zero, so pure-translation twists have zero "length" — no fair ruler. Constraint panel: a pink tool pushing on a slate wall: free motions (lime) and constraint wrenches (purple) keep zero work under any frame change, while "dot-product orthogonal" twists fail. Manipulability panel: the same arm with two tool frames shows different σmin readouts.

scenes.title: Fair Volume
scenes.brief: A box spanned by n orange arrows; its gold volume readout = det. A map with Jacobian J scales the box by det J (pull-back). For SE(3): apply Ad_h to a 6-arrow box — the 6D volume meter stays exactly 1× however you drag h (lime), unlike the metric panel. SO(3) panel: fill a ball of radius π with rotation vectors; total volume counter → 8π³. Arm panel: a 6R arm sweeps its reachable poses; a work-volume bar compares against the bound (4/3)π L³ · 8π³; morph through designs — elbow arms with the elbow midway hit the bound (gold crown), others leave a hole.

pages.summary: Appendix A introduces Lie groups as the hidden backbone of the book's rigid-body tools, starting with smooth maps, diffeomorphisms, charts and atlases.

atoms.idea: Appendix A title: Lie groups and robot kinematics.
Most analytic tools of the book come from Lie group theory and Riemannian geometry; this appendix gives the basics and ties them to rigid-body kinematics.
atoms.feynman: The tricks you learned for spinning and sliding objects all come from one toolbox, like recipes that all start from the same dough.
atoms.visual: Zoo entrance: a gold arch with chapter-2/3 icons (rotation, twist, Jacobian) as lanterns; tapping each lights the cage of the group it lives in.

atoms.idea: Section A.1: differentiable manifolds.
A short review of differential geometry, following a standard text [9], mainly to set notation.
atoms.feynman: Before a trip we agree on what "north" and "a mile" mean.
atoms.visual: The paper-map globe fades in with an empty legend; each notation symbol later added to the legend glows when used.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.1.1: manifolds and maps.

A map between open subsets of Euclidean spaces is smooth if all partial derivatives of every order exist and are continuous; a diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse (same dimension).
atoms.feynman: Stretching a rubber sheet without tearing or creasing, and being able to un-stretch it the same way.
atoms.visual: A flat orange grid gets warped by a draggable smooth map into a pink grid; a lime "smooth" badge stays on; an "undo" arrow maps it back exactly. Add a fold: the badge turns coral (not invertible).

atoms.idea: An n-dimensional manifold looks locally like Rⁿ; charts (φ,U) send pieces to open sets of Rⁿ; two overlapping charts are compatible when the overlap (change-of-map) function between them is a diffeomorphism; an atlas of compatible charts covering M makes it a smooth manifold.
atoms.feynman: A globe covered by flat paper maps: every spot is on some map, and where two maps overlap you can translate between them smoothly.
atoms.visual: Globe with 4–6 blue paper caps. Hover a teal point: its image lights on every map containing it. In an overlap, a purple warped mini-grid shows the transition map; a lime smoothness meter confirms compatibility. Remove a cap: an uncovered coral hole appears (not an atlas).

atoms.idea: Page 403

pages.summary: Smooth maps between manifolds via charts; tangent vectors as derivations with a coordinate basis; the tangent map and its chain rule.

atoms.idea: A map F between manifolds is smooth (or a diffeomorphism) when, read through any charts, ψ∘F∘φ⁻¹ is smooth (or a diffeomorphism) between flat sets.
atoms.feynman: To check a road trip between two planets is smooth, read it on the flat maps of each planet; if the map-to-map drawing has no jumps, the trip is smooth.
atoms.visual: Globe → donut with an orange map F; side panels show the two flat charts and the induced flat-to-flat warp; dragging a point traces matched dots in all four views.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.1.2: tangent spaces and tangent maps.
A derivation at p is a real-valued operator on functions smooth near p that is linear and satisfies the product (Leibniz) rule X(fg) = (Xf)g(p) + f(p)(Xg).
atoms.feynman: Asking "how fast does the temperature rise if I walk this way?" — double the heat, double the answer; for a product of two things, each one's change counts weighted by the other.
atoms.visual: Ball with a gold temperature map and a second teal humidity map; an orange arrow at p; readouts Xf, Xg, X(fg) and a lime check showing X(fg) = Xf·g + f·Xg live as the arrow is dragged.

atoms.idea: Derivations at p can be added and scaled, so they form a real vector space.
atoms.feynman: Two walking directions can be combined into one, and the rates of change add up the same way.
atoms.visual: Two orange arrows on the touching sheet; their sum (pink, tip-to-tail) has readout equal to the sum of readouts.

atoms.idea: The tangent space T_pM is the set of all derivations at p (tangent vectors); in a chart, the partials ∂/∂xᵢ form a basis, so each tangent vector has coordinates (X₁,…,Xₙ).
atoms.feynman: The flat sheet of paper that touches a ball at one point: every way you could start rolling from that point is an arrow on the sheet.
atoms.visual: Touching sheet on the ball at a draggable p; red ∂/∂x₁ and green ∂/∂x₂ arrows along the chart grid lines; an orange arrow X decomposes into X₁, X₂ with two number readouts that change when you switch charts while the arrow stays put.

atoms.idea: The tangent map F_* (also T_pF) of a smooth F sends a tangent vector at p to one at F(p) by F_*X(f) = X(f∘F); in coordinates it is the Jacobian matrix.
atoms.feynman: Push a toy boat along a stretchy river: where the river is stretched, the boat's speed arrow gets longer.
atoms.visual: Ball → egg map; an orange arrow at p is carried to a pink arrow at F(p); the 2×2 Jacobian tiles beside it multiply the coordinates live.

atoms.idea: Tangent maps obey the chain rule: the tangent map of F∘G is the tangent map of F (at G(p)) after that of G.
atoms.feynman: Two zoom lenses in a row magnify by the product of their zooms.
atoms.visual: Two maps G then F; the arrow is pushed twice (orange → blue → pink); a lime check shows it matches pushing once through F∘G; Jacobian tiles multiply.

atoms.idea: Page 404

pages.summary: Diffeomorphisms give invertible tangent maps; tangent maps via curves; the tangent bundle; cotangent vectors, differentials and cotangent maps.

atoms.idea: If F is a diffeomorphism, each tangent map is an invertible linear map whose inverse is the tangent map of F⁻¹.
atoms.feynman: If you can un-stretch the rubber, you can also un-stretch every arrow drawn on it.
atoms.visual: Ball ↔ egg with a reverse arrow; push an arrow forward then back; it returns to its exact start (lime) and the Jacobian tiles × inverse tiles = identity.

atoms.idea: If a curve c through p has velocity X at time 0, then the pushed vector is the time derivative of F(c(t)) at 0.
atoms.feynman: An ant walks on the balloon; its speed on the inflated balloon is its speed seen after inflation.
atoms.visual: A teal ant walks a curve through p; the same ant drawn on the egg; both velocity arrows are shown, the pink one equals the pushed orange one.

atoms.idea: The tangent bundle TM is the 2n-dimensional manifold of all pairs (p, X_p), with projection π back to the base point.
atoms.feynman: A hairbrush: the handle is the manifold and every bristle is the sheet of possible velocities at that spot.
atoms.visual: Circle manifold with a tangent line at each point stood up vertically, forming a cylinder (TS¹); dragging a (point, arrow) pair moves on the cylinder and a dashed π line drops to the base circle.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.1.3: cotangent spaces and cotangent maps.
The cotangent space T*_pM is the dual of T_pM: linear functions ω eating tangent vectors; the dual basis dxᵢ satisfies ⟨dxᵢ, ∂/∂xⱼ⟩ = δᵢⱼ.
atoms.feynman: A price list: a cart of groceries (vector) goes in, a total price (number) comes out; the price of "one apple" is the dual basis item.
atoms.visual: Purple stacks of parallel lines on the touching sheet; drop an orange arrow — the lines-crossed counter shows ⟨ω, X⟩. Basis stacks dx₁, dx₂ cross the red/green basis arrows exactly once each (1/0 badges).

atoms.idea: The differential df(p) of a function f is the covector with ⟨df, X⟩ = Xf; in coordinates df = Σ ∂f/∂xᵢ dxᵢ.
atoms.feynman: On a hiking map, the contour lines near you tell how many height steps you cross for any short walk.
atoms.visual: Gold hill with contour lines; zoom at p until contours become a straight purple stack = df(p); an orange walking arrow's crossing count equals the height change readout.

atoms.idea: The cotangent map F^* goes backward: it pulls a covector at F(p) to one at p by ⟨F^*α, X⟩ = ⟨α, F_*X⟩ (transpose of the Jacobian).
atoms.feynman: Translate a foreign price list into your home currency so totals agree whichever side you compute them on.
atoms.visual: Arrow pushed forward (orange→pink) while a purple stack on the target is pulled back to the source; the two crossing counters stay equal (lime). Jacobian tiles flip to their transpose.

atoms.idea: Page 405

pages.summary: The cotangent bundle; vector fields as sections and as differential equations; integral curves and flows; the Lie derivative of a function.

atoms.idea: The cotangent bundle T*M collects all cotangent spaces into a 2n-dimensional manifold of pairs (p, α_p).
atoms.feynman: A hairbrush again, but each bristle now holds price lists instead of arrows.
atoms.visual: The TS¹ cylinder recolored purple: each vertical line now holds covector stacks; a dragged (p, α) pair slides on it.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.1.4: vector fields.
A smooth vector field assigns smoothly to each point p a tangent vector at p (a section with π∘X = id); in coordinates it is a column of n smooth functions.
atoms.feynman: A weather map with a wind arrow at every town, and nearby towns have similar winds.
atoms.visual: A plane or sphere filled with orange arrows; hovering a point shows its column (X₁(x), X₂(x)) readout; a smoothness slider blends neighboring arrows.

atoms.idea: A vector field is a differential equation: a curve is an integral curve if its velocity always equals the field at its position.
atoms.feynman: A leaf dropped on a stream goes wherever the water under it points.
atoms.visual: Drop a teal leaf; it follows the arrows by RK4, leaving a trail; its velocity arrow (pink) always overlaps the field arrow under it.

atoms.idea: ODE theory gives local integral curves; if they exist for all time the field is complete and they define a flow Φ_t, a one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms.
atoms.feynman: Pour a sheet of glitter onto the river: after t seconds every speck has moved, and the whole pattern moved together without tearing.
atoms.visual: A grid of teal dots flows as a time slider runs; the deformed grid stays untorn; Φ_s then Φ_t equals Φ_{s+t} (lime check). A field that blows up in finite time shows dots escaping off-screen (coral, not complete).

atoms.idea: The Lie derivative of a function f along X is the new function Xf(p) = X_p f: the rate of change of f as you drift with the field.
atoms.feynman: Riding the wind in a balloon, how fast does the temperature you feel change?
atoms.visual: Gold temperature colors on the plane; riding leaf shows a thermometer readout and its rate bar; the rate bar matches the color of Xf painted as a second layer.
atoms.beat: 📈 rate of change along the flow

atoms.idea: Page 406

pages.summary: Lie derivative in coordinates; the Lie bracket of vector fields and its coordinate formula; F-related fields, push forward and pull back; brackets are preserved; Lie algebra axioms begin.

atoms.idea: In coordinates, Xf = Σᵢ (∂f/∂xᵢ) Xᵢ: gradient of f dotted with the field.
atoms.feynman: How fast your height changes = how steep each direction is × how fast you go that way, added up.
atoms.visual: Readout panel: gradient arrow of f (gold) and field arrow (orange) at the leaf; their dot product bar equals the rate bar from the previous beat.
atoms.beat: 📈 rate of change along the flow

atoms.idea: The Lie bracket [X,Y] is the vector field acting on functions by X(Yf) − Y(Xf).
atoms.feynman: Put on socks then shoes vs. shoes then socks: the difference in outcome measures how much the order matters.
atoms.visual: Two fields X (orange) and Y (blue); flow X·ε, Y·ε, −X·ε, −Y·ε from a point; a coral gap vector remains; ÷ε² it converges to a pink arrow = [X,Y].

atoms.idea: The bracket is again a derivation, and in coordinates [X,Y]ⱼ = Σᵢ (∂Yⱼ/∂xᵢ Xᵢ − ∂Xⱼ/∂xᵢ Yᵢ), i.e. (DY)X − (DX)Y.
atoms.feynman: How much Y's arrows change as you move along X, minus how much X's arrows change along Y.
atoms.visual: At a point, the two Jacobian tile grids DX, DY; arrows DY·X and DX·Y drawn; their difference (pink) overlays the loop-gap arrow from the previous beat (lime match).

atoms.idea: Fields X on M and Y on N are F-related if pushing X at p by F gives Y at F(p).
atoms.feynman: A shadow puppet: the hand's motion and the shadow's motion match through the lamp's projection.
atoms.visual: Left plane with field X, right plane with field Y; F maps between; at sample points pushed orange arrows overlay blue Y arrows (lime) or not (coral).

atoms.idea: A diffeomorphism F pushes a whole field forward, (F_*X)_q = F_* X at F⁻¹(q); the pull back F^* = (F⁻¹)_* goes the other way.
atoms.feynman: Redraw the wind map after the continents are stretched: every arrow is carried to the new spot and stretched with the land.
atoms.visual: Orange field on a grid; an F warp slider deforms the grid and the arrows ride along (pink); reverse slider pulls them back identically.

atoms.label: Prop A.1
atoms.idea: Pushing forward respects brackets: F_*[X,Y] = [F_*X, F_*Y].
atoms.feynman: If you rename the streets of a town, the shortcut you find by going around a block is the same shortcut under the new names.
atoms.visual: Compute the bracket loop on the original grid and on the warped grid; the warped pink gap arrow equals the pushed original (lime check).

atoms.idea: A Lie algebra is a vector space with a bilinear bracket that is skew-symmetric ([v,w] = −[w,v]) and satisfies Jacobi (next page).
atoms.feynman: Swapping the order of two moves flips the leftover gap to point the opposite way.
atoms.visual: Bracket panel: swap X and Y and the pink gap arrow flips 180°.

atoms.idea: Page 407

pages.summary: Jacobi identity, Lie subalgebras, one-forms and their pull back; Lie groups defined, with left and right translations.

atoms.idea: Jacobi identity: [[v,w],z] + [[z,v],w] + [[w,z],v] = 0.
atoms.feynman: Three kids pass a ball in a circle in three orders; the leftover wobbles cancel out perfectly.
atoms.visual: Three cross-product arrows in 3D (cyclic double brackets) placed tip-to-tail close into a triangle; a lime "0" readout; dragging v, w, z keeps it closed.

atoms.idea: A subalgebra is closed under bracket; smooth vector fields on M form an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra.
atoms.feynman: A club whose members' handshakes only ever introduce other members.
atoms.visual: A family of fields shown as cards; bracketing two cards produces a card that lands inside (lime ring) or outside (coral) the chosen family.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.1.5: differential forms.
A one-form assigns smoothly to each point a covector: α = Σ αᵢ(x) dxᵢ.
atoms.feynman: A field of price lists, one at every shop, changing gently from shop to shop.
atoms.visual: Purple covector stacks drawn at grid points, their spacing and tilt varying smoothly.

atoms.idea: Any smooth map F (not necessarily invertible) pulls a one-form β on N back to F^*β on M by ⟨F^*β, X⟩ = ⟨β, F_*X⟩.
atoms.feynman: You can always ask "what does this walk cost on the far map?" even if the map squashes many places onto one.
atoms.visual: A non-invertible map (plane → line squash); pulled-back purple stacks appear on the source; crossing counters match on both sides.

atoms.idea: Section A.2: Lie groups.
Lie-group basics for kinematics; further detail in [108], explicit SO(3)/SE(3) formulas in [88].
atoms.feynman: A quick tour with pointers to bigger guidebooks.
atoms.visual: Zoo map with signposts to the cages for SO(3) and SE(3).

atoms.idea: Subsection A.2.1: definition and examples.
A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion; abelian if order never matters; e is the identity.
atoms.feynman: Turns of a steering wheel: you can combine turns, undo them, and nudge them a tiny bit smoothly.
atoms.visual: Circle cage: drag g and h; gh moves smoothly as you drag; an inverse ghost mirrors g; e is a gold dot. An abelian badge is lime here, coral in the SO(3) cage (gh ≠ hg).

atoms.idea: Left translation L_g(h) = gh and right translation R_g(h) = hg.
atoms.feynman: Moving a chess piece by the board's directions (left) vs. by the piece's own facing (right).
atoms.visual: SE(2) cage: a car-shaped frame h; L_g moves it by world arrows, R_g moves it along its own nose; two ghosts show both results.

atoms.idea: Page 408

pages.summary: Translations are commuting diffeomorphisms; examples Rⁿ, GL(n), SO(n) (dimension n(n−1)/2) and SE(3) (dimension 6); left-invariant vector fields.

atoms.idea: Translations compose into translations (L_g∘L_h = L_gh), so each has an inverse translation and is a diffeomorphism; left and right translations commute; in abelian groups they coincide.
atoms.feynman: Rearranging the room by world directions and rearranging each chair by its own facing don't interfere with each other.
atoms.visual: SE(2) cage: apply L_g then R_h, and R_h then L_g; two ghost frames land on the same spot (lime); in the Rⁿ cage the two buttons do identical things.

atoms.label: Ex A.1
atoms.idea: Rⁿ with addition is an abelian Lie group (identity 0, inverse −x).
atoms.feynman: Sliding a book across a table: slides add, and order never matters.
atoms.visual: Plane cage: two orange slide arrows added in either order reach the same pink spot.

atoms.label: Ex A.2
atoms.idea: GL(n,R), invertible n×n matrices under multiplication, is an open subset of R^{n²} with smooth product and inverse.
atoms.feynman: All the ways to stretch, shear and turn a rubber grid without squashing it flat.
atoms.visual: GL(2) cage: drag î, ĵ columns; the grid deforms; a det readout; at det = 0 the grid collapses to a line and the cage bars turn coral (left the group).

atoms.label: Ex A.3
atoms.idea: SO(n) = orthogonal matrices with det +1, a subgroup of dimension n(n−1)/2; SO(3) is the rotation group.
atoms.feynman: All the ways to turn a ball without denting or mirroring it: three turning knobs for 3D.
atoms.visual: SO(3) cage: a blue ball with red/green/blue axes; dimension counter shows 3 for n=3, 1 for n=2, 6 for n=4 (number of planes of turning).

atoms.label: Ex A.4
atoms.idea: SE(3): maps x ↦ Rx + p, written as 4×4 matrices [[R,p],[0,1]]; a 6-dimensional Lie group.
atoms.feynman: Picking up a mug and putting it down somewhere else, turned: three ways to turn plus three ways to slide.
atoms.visual: SE(3) cage: a floating frame; 4×4 tiles (R block blue, p column teal); drag to move; dimension counter 3+3 = 6.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.2.2: the Lie algebra of a Lie group.
A vector field X on G is left invariant if pushing it by any left translation leaves it unchanged: T_hL_g X(h) = X(gh).
atoms.feynman: A marching band where everyone takes the same step relative to themselves: if you shift the whole band, the step pattern looks the same.
atoms.visual: Group surface with orange arrows; applying L_g moves every arrow to a new spot and it lands exactly on the arrow already there (lime overlap).

atoms.idea: Page 409

pages.summary: Left-invariant fields form a subalgebra isomorphic to the tangent space at the identity, which becomes the Lie algebra; Rⁿ has the trivial bracket; GL(n) begins.

atoms.idea: Brackets of left-invariant fields are left invariant, so they form a Lie subalgebra of all vector fields.
atoms.feynman: Two marching patterns that look the same from every spot produce a leftover drift that also looks the same from every spot.
atoms.visual: Run the bracket loop at several points of the left-invariant fields; the pink gap arrows are copies of one another under L_g.

atoms.idea: Each vector ξ at the identity defines X_ξ(g) = T_eL_g ξ, which is left invariant because L_gh = L_g∘L_h.
atoms.feynman: Decide one dance step at home, then everyone copies it relative to where they stand.
atoms.visual: Gold home e with an orange arrow ξ; "copy" button sweeps the arrow over the group by left translation, painting a full field.

atoms.label: Eq (A.1)
atoms.idea: Evaluating at e and copying from e are inverse linear maps, so left-invariant fields ≅ T_eG; defining [ξ₁,ξ₂] = [X_ξ₁, X_ξ₂](e) makes T_eG the Lie algebra 𝔤.
atoms.feynman: A whole wind pattern is decided by one arrow at home; the twist you get by mixing two patterns is also read off at home.
atoms.visual: Split view: the full field and the single home arrow, linked by two buttons (restrict ↔ copy) that undo each other; the bracket gap at home is pinned as a pink arrow in the home sheet.

atoms.idea: A Lie subgroup H has a Lie algebra that is a subalgebra of 𝔤.
atoms.feynman: The turns that keep the floor flat (spinning about vertical) are a smaller club, and mixing them never takes you out of the club.
atoms.visual: In SO(3), restrict arrows to the z-axis line; brackets stay on that line (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.5
atoms.idea: For Rⁿ, left-invariant fields are constant fields and the bracket is identically zero.
atoms.feynman: Sliding moves never interfere: slide east then north = north then east.
atoms.visual: Plane cage: uniform arrow field; the bracket loop closes exactly, gap readout 0 (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.6
atoms.idea: The Lie algebra of GL(n) is all n×n matrices with bracket [A,B] = AB − BA; it comes from coordinates xᵢⱼ on the open set GL ⊂ R^{n×n}.
atoms.feynman: Order of two shears matters, and the commutator measures exactly by how much.
atoms.visual: GL(2) cage: two small orange matrices A, B as grid nudges; AB and BA results side by side; their difference AB−BA drawn as a pink grid nudge.

atoms.idea: Page 410

pages.summary: so(3) as skew matrices whose bracket is the cross product; se(3) as 4×4 twist matrices with an explicit bracket, identified with R⁶.

atoms.label: Ex A.6
atoms.idea: The commutator formula follows from computing left-invariant fields on GL and applying (A.1); details in [108].
atoms.feynman: The rule was found by actually running the go-go-back-back loop on matrices.
atoms.visual: Bracket loop on GL(2) with tiny ε: (e^{εA}e^{εB}e^{−εA}e^{−εB} − I)/ε² converges to AB − BA (lime match readout).

atoms.label: Ex A.7, Eq (A.2)
atoms.idea: so(3) = 3×3 skew-symmetric matrices ω̂ (Eq A.2) with commutator bracket; the hat map makes (R³, ×) and (so(3), [·,·]) isomorphic: [ω̂₁, ω̂₂] = (ω₁×ω₂)^.
atoms.feynman: Tilt a phone forward then roll it, and undo in the other order: the leftover is a small turn about the third axis — exactly the cross product.
atoms.visual: Two orange ω arrows in 3D; the 3×3 hat tiles light up entry by entry; commutator tiles shown next to the hat of the pink ω₁×ω₂ arrow — identical (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.8
atoms.idea: se(3) = 4×4 matrices [[ω̂, v],[0,0]] with commutator bracket [ξ₁,ξ₂] = ((ω₁×ω₂)^, ω₁×v₂ − ω₂×v₁); isomorphic to R⁶ via (v, ω).
atoms.feynman: Two screwdriver twists done in a loop leave a leftover screw whose spin is the cross of spins and whose slide mixes each spin with the other's slide.
atoms.visual: Two gold screw axes with pitch; bracket loop runs; the leftover screw (pink) axis plus readouts for its ω and v parts match the formula tiles.

atoms.idea: Page 411

pages.summary: Integral curves of left-invariant fields are one-parameter subgroups; the exponential map, its rescaling property and local invertibility; exp on Rⁿ and on GL(n).

atoms.idea: Subsection A.2.3: the exponential map.
The integral curve φ_ξ of X_ξ through e satisfies φ_ξ(s+t) = φ_ξ(s)φ_ξ(t): a one-parameter subgroup.
atoms.feynman: Turning a knob steadily: 2 seconds then 3 seconds of turning equals 5 seconds of turning.
atoms.visual: Home e, arrow ξ; the curve φ_ξ grows; add-times widget: pick s and t; ghost frames at φ(s)φ(t) and φ(s+t) coincide (lime).

atoms.idea: Proof: both sides start equal at t=0 and solve the same left-invariant ODE, so uniqueness forces equality; the same property extends the curve to all t.
atoms.feynman: Two leaves dropped at the same spot on the same stream must follow the same path.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) two curves start at the same dot; (2) both obey the same arrows (field shown); (3) they overlap forever (lime); (4) chain copies to extend the curve without end.

atoms.idea: exp(ξ) = φ_ξ(1); it sends the line ξs in 𝔤 onto the one-parameter subgroup: exp(ξs) = φ_ξ(s).
atoms.feynman: Hold the throttle at setting ξ for exactly one second: where you land is exp(ξ).
atoms.visual: Slider s scales the orange arrow; the pink endpoint frame exp(ξs) slides along the same curve.

atoms.idea: Rescaling: t ↦ φ_ξ(ts) solves the ODE of sξ, so φ_{sξ}(t) = φ_ξ(ts); set t=1. All connected one-parameter subgroups arise this way.
atoms.feynman: Driving twice as fast for one hour lands you where driving normal speed for two hours does.
atoms.visual: Two ghosts: speed 2ξ for t=1 and speed ξ for t=2 trace the same curve; badge lime.

atoms.idea: The derivative of exp at 0 is the identity, so exp is a local diffeomorphism near 0 → near e (inverse function theorem); for compact groups exp is onto.
atoms.feynman: Very small throttle settings land very close to home, one-to-one; and for a spinning ball you can reach every orientation.
atoms.visual: Small disc of arrows near 0 maps onto a small patch around e with no overlaps (grid stays a grid); for SO(3) a sweep of all ξ fills every orientation (coverage meter 100%).

atoms.label: Ex A.9
atoms.idea: For Rⁿ the integral curve is x + vt, so exp is the identity map.
atoms.feynman: In a flat parking lot, driving straight at velocity v for one second just adds v.
atoms.visual: Plane cage: arrow v and its exp endpoint coincide (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.10
atoms.idea: For GL(n), Φ_A(t) = Σ tⁿAⁿ/n! is a one-parameter subgroup (starts at I).
atoms.feynman: Compound interest done continuously: tiny growths on growths add up to an exponential.
atoms.visual: Series panel: stacked bars for terms tᵏAᵏ/k! appear one by one and their sum converges (bar heights shrink).

atoms.idea: Page 412

pages.summary: Matrix exponential series; Rodrigues formula on SO(3) (A.3); exponential on SE(3); local log; log series on GL(n).

atoms.label: Ex A.10
atoms.idea: Differentiating the series gives Φ̇ = Φ A, so Φ_A is the integral curve of the left-invariant field; hence exp(A) = Σ Aⁿ/n!.
atoms.feynman: Your growth rate is always "current amount × A", the defining habit of an exponential.
atoms.visual: n small steps (I + A/n)ⁿ drawn as ghost grids converging to the series result; a lime error bar shrinks as n grows.

atoms.label: Ex A.11, Eq (A.3)
atoms.idea: On SO(3), exp(ω̂) rotates by angle ‖ω‖ about ω, with the closed Rodrigues formula I + sin‖ω‖ ω̂/‖ω‖ + (1−cos‖ω‖) ω̂²/‖ω‖².
atoms.feynman: A sticker on a spinning top: its path is a circle, so all you need is a sine and a cosine.
atoms.visual: Spin mode: orange ω arrow; a blue body rotates; sin and cos dials feed the formula tiles; the result matches the many-step product (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.12
atoms.idea: On SE(3), exp of [[ω̂, v],[0,0]] is [[I, v],[0,1]] if ω = 0, otherwise [[e^{ω̂}, A v],[0,1]] with A = I + (1−cos‖ω‖) ω̂/‖ω‖² + (‖ω‖ − sin‖ω‖) ω̂²/‖ω‖³.
atoms.feynman: A screw: turning while advancing; the advance is bent along the turn, which is what matrix A accounts for.
atoms.visual: Screw mode: a frame corkscrews along a gold axis; the A·v translation drawn as a curved teal path; ω→0 slider shows the path straighten into pure slide.

atoms.idea: Since exp is a local diffeomorphism, there is a local inverse log near e with exp(log g) = g; for GL(n) it can be written explicitly.
atoms.feynman: Rewind: given where you ended up, find which steady throttle setting got you there.
atoms.visual: Log mode: drag a pink target frame near home; the scene solves for ξ and replays exp(ξ) landing on it.

atoms.label: Ex A.13
atoms.idea: For GL(n), log A = Σ (−1)^{n+1}(A − I)ⁿ/n, converging when ‖A − I‖ < 1.
atoms.feynman: Undo compound interest by a series that works only when the growth was not too big.
atoms.visual: Series bars for log converge for targets inside a lime disc around I and blow up (coral) outside.

atoms.idea: Page 413

pages.summary: Log formulas on SO(3) and SE(3), both multi-valued; canonical coordinates of the first kind and an atlas built by left translation.

atoms.label: Ex A.14
atoms.idea: On SO(3), log R = θω̂ with 2cosθ + 1 = trace R and ω̂ = (R − Rᵀ)/(2 sinθ) for R ≠ I; at R = I any axis works and θ = 2πk: log is multi-valued.
atoms.feynman: Read how far a wheel turned from where the valve ended up — but an extra full turn looks identical.
atoms.visual: Pink target rotation; θ read from a trace gauge; ω axis appears; ghost solutions at θ+2π and (−ω, 2π−θ) land on the same orientation.

atoms.label: Ex A.15
atoms.idea: On SE(3), log [[R,p],[0,1]] = [[ω̂, A⁻¹p],[0,0]] with ω̂ = log R and a closed form for A⁻¹; also multi-valued.
atoms.feynman: Find the single screw that moves the mug from here to there; there may be several equivalent screws.
atoms.visual: Drag the pink target frame; the solved gold screw axis appears with its pitch; a second solution ghost path also lands on target.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.2.4: canonical coordinates on a Lie group.

atoms.label: Eq (A.4)
atoms.idea: With a basis X₁..Xₙ of 𝔤, g = exp(Σ σᵢXᵢ) gives local coordinates σ near e (canonical coordinates of the first kind).
atoms.feynman: Describe any nearby orientation by one combined "turn this much about this blended axis" instruction.
atoms.visual: Three orange σ sliders build a blended arrow; one straight exp path from home reaches the pink frame; a small coordinate grid around home warps onto the group.

atoms.idea: Left-translating that chart gives charts ψ_g(h) = σ(g⁻¹h) around every g, forming an atlas; σ are the canonical coordinates of the first kind.
atoms.feynman: Carry your home neighborhood map with you: wherever you stand, measure from there.
atoms.visual: Tile beat: the coordinate patch at home is copied by L_g to several places on the SO(3) ball until patches cover it (paper-map globe callback).

atoms.idea: Page 414

pages.summary: Canonical coordinates of the second kind (POE, Euler angles); left actions, orbits; GL acting on Rⁿ, conjugation and the adjoint action.

atoms.label: Eq (A.5)
atoms.idea: Writing g = e^{X₁θ₁}⋯e^{Xₙθₙ} near e gives canonical coordinates of the second kind; examples are the product-of-exponentials formula and Euler angles.
atoms.feynman: A robot arm: each joint turns about its own fixed axis one after another, and the list of joint angles describes where the hand is.
atoms.visual: Second-kind mode: three θ sliders each spin about a fixed axis in turn; the three-segment path lands on the same pink frame as the first-kind straight path; a robot-arm skin can be toggled on.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.2.5: actions of Lie groups.
All chapter-2 transformations of points, vectors, twists and wrenches are left actions of SE(3) on suitable spaces.
atoms.feynman: One choreographer (the rigid motion), many dancers of different kinds — dots, arrows, screws, pushes — each following the matching rule.
atoms.visual: Dance floor with four dancer kinds (teal points, orange arrows, gold screws, purple wrenches); one g knob moves all of them by their own rules.

atoms.idea: A left action Φ: G×M → M satisfies Φ(e,x) = x and Φ(g,Φ(h,x)) = Φ(gh,x); the orbit of x is everything it can be moved to.
atoms.feynman: Everyone in a dance moves by the same rule; doing two moves in a row equals the combined move; all spots one dancer can reach form its orbit.
atoms.visual: Teal points on the floor; identity knob leaves them still; "h then g" vs "gh" buttons land on identical spots (lime). Sweep g: one dancer paints its orbit (a circle for rotations).

atoms.label: Ex A.16
atoms.idea: GL(n) acts on Rⁿ by matrix-vector product; the orbit of any nonzero x is Rⁿ minus the origin.
atoms.feynman: Stretch and turn a rubber sheet every possible way: a dot can be sent anywhere except the pinned center.
atoms.visual: Plane with a teal dot; random GL(2) samples scatter it everywhere (orbit fills plane) while the origin stays fixed (slate pin).

atoms.label: Ex A.17
atoms.idea: Conjugation I_g(h) = ghg⁻¹ is an action of G on itself; its orbits are similarity classes.
atoms.feynman: Describe a dance move from a friend's seat: same move, seen from another viewpoint.
atoms.visual: A motion h shown as a gold screw; move the viewer with g; the conjugated screw ghg⁻¹ is the same screw moved by g (pitch and angle readouts unchanged).

atoms.label: Ex A.18
atoms.idea: Differentiating conjugation at e gives the adjoint action Ad_g on 𝔤; for matrix groups Ad_g ξ = gξg⁻¹.
atoms.feynman: Re-describe an instruction like "twist here" from a different person's point of view.
atoms.visual: An orange twist arrow at home; moving the viewpoint g re-expresses it; 6×6 Ad tiles light up and multiply the twist coordinates.

atoms.idea: Page 415

pages.summary: Coadjoint and lifted actions; the Euclidean group section begins: rigid configurations compose by the group product.

atoms.label: Ex A.19
atoms.idea: The coadjoint action on the dual 𝔤*: Ad*_g is the transpose of Ad_g, and g acts on covectors by Ad*_{g⁻¹} so pairings are preserved.
atoms.feynman: If prices are re-labelled when goods are re-labelled, the bill total stays the same.
atoms.visual: A purple wrench and an orange twist; move the viewpoint g: the twist transforms by Ad, the wrench by the inverse-transpose; a work readout ⟨F, V⟩ stays frozen (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.20
atoms.idea: An action on M lifts to TM: a point moves by Φ_g and its tangent arrow by the tangent map of Φ_g.
atoms.feynman: When dancers turn, the direction each one is walking turns with them.
atoms.visual: Each teal dancer carries a small orange velocity arrow; turning the g knob rotates and carries the arrows along (pink).

atoms.idea: Section A.3: the geometry of the Euclidean group.
This section studies SE(3)'s geometry and what it means for kinematics and control, drawing on [63] and [59, 77, 86].
atoms.feynman: Now we zoom into the one cage of the zoo that robots live in.
atoms.visual: Zoo camera flies into the SE(3) cage, which fills the screen.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.3.1: basic properties.
Chapter-2 rigid-motion tools (homogeneous matrices, screws) are special cases of general Lie-group tools.
atoms.feynman: The special kitchen gadgets you used turn out to be one universal tool with different attachments.
atoms.visual: Chapter-2 icons (4×4 matrix, screw, twist) slide into labelled slots of the general Lie-group machine diagram (group, algebra, exp, Ad).

atoms.idea: Subheading: rigid body kinematics.
A configuration g_ab = (p_ab, R_ab) gives frame B relative to A; composing through an intermediate frame: g_ac = g_ab g_bc = (p_ab + R_ab p_bc, R_ab R_bc).
atoms.feynman: Directions from home to the park, then from the park to the shop, add up to directions from home to the shop.
atoms.visual: Three frames A (slate), B, C (blue); drag B and C; the composed arrow chain A→B→C equals the direct pink A→C frame; formula tiles update.

atoms.idea: Page 416

pages.summary: SE(3) as a subgroup of GL(4); actions on points (homogeneous 1) and on velocities (homogeneous 0); twists as the Lie algebra se(3).

atoms.idea: As 4×4 homogeneous matrices, SE(3) composition is matrix multiplication, making it a subgroup of GL(4).
atoms.feynman: Stacking transparencies: each sheet is a move, and laying them on top of each other multiplies them.
atoms.visual: 4×4 tile matrices multiply as you chain frames; the bottom row stays [0 0 0 1] (lime lock icon).

atoms.idea: g_ab also converts point coordinates from B to A: q_a = p + R q_b; in homogeneous form (q,1) this is a matrix-vector product, and associativity makes it an action.
atoms.feynman: The same lamp described from two corners of the room: different numbers, same lamp.
atoms.visual: A teal point on the body, with its B-coordinates and A-coordinates shown; appending a "1" slot lets the 4×4 matrix move it — translation applies.

atoms.idea: Velocities of points are tangent vectors; SE(3) acts on them by the lifted action (rotate only), written in homogeneous form with a 0 in the last slot.
atoms.feynman: An arrow painted on a moving cart turns with the cart but does not get carried off by the cart's slide.
atoms.visual: Toggle the 4th slot of an orange arrow between 1 and 0: with 1 it gets translated (wrong for a velocity, coral), with 0 it only rotates (lime).

atoms.idea: se(3) is the subalgebra of gl(4) of matrices [[ω̂, v],[0,0]] with commutator bracket; its elements are twists, a 6-dimensional space ≅ R⁶.
atoms.feynman: A twist is a "how fast and which way" instruction for a rigid body: three turning rates and three sliding rates.
atoms.visual: 4×4 twist tiles (ω̂ in red/green/blue skew block, v in teal column, zero bottom row); six sliders drive them; exp sends it to a moving frame.

atoms.idea: Twists have a screw interpretation: rotating and translating simultaneously about an axis through q in direction ω.
atoms.feynman: A bolt being screwed in: it turns and advances along one line at the same time.
atoms.visual: A gold axis through a draggable point q with direction ω; a bolt mesh rides it.

atoms.idea: Page 417

pages.summary: Twists from screw axis and pitch; exp onto SE(3) restates Chasles; exp is not one-to-one; velocities on a Lie group translate to the Lie algebra; tangent map of left translation is matrix multiplication.

atoms.idea: With pitch h, the screw twist is [[ω̂, −ω×q + hω],[0,0]]; exp(ξθ) rotates about the axis and translates along it: a screw motion.
atoms.feynman: A drill bit going into wood: how far it advances per turn is the pitch.
atoms.visual: Pitch slider (h): the bolt mesh advances h per radian; at h=0 pure spin, large h nearly pure slide; the twist tiles update.

atoms.idea: Near e every element is exp of a twist; for SE(3) exp is in fact onto, so every rigid motion is a screw motion (Chasles).
atoms.feynman: Any way you move a book from one place to another could also be done by a single corkscrew motion.
atoms.visual: Drag a pink target placement of a book anywhere; the gold screw axis that does it in one smooth corkscrew appears and animates.

atoms.idea: exp is not one-to-one, so twists don't parameterize SE(3): e.g. angle θ about ω equals 2π−θ about −ω.
atoms.feynman: Turning a doorknob 270° right lands where 90° left does.
atoms.visual: Two ghost screws (orange θ about ω, blue 2π−θ about −ω) both end on the same pink frame.

atoms.idea: Subheading: velocities and forces.
A curve's velocity lives in the tangent space at its current point; on a Lie group it can be translated back to the identity, giving a Lie-algebra element.
atoms.feynman: Describe a moving car's speed by imagining it was parked at home and given the same push.
atoms.visual: Moving frame g(t) with its tangent arrow; a "bring home" button left-translates the arrow to the gold home sheet as a twist.

atoms.idea: On matrix groups, the tangent map of L_h is left multiplication: T_gL_h X_g = hX_g (via d/dt of h·g(t)).
atoms.feynman: Moving the whole film reel doesn't change the movie's speed, it just relocates it.
atoms.visual: Curve g(t) and its moved copy h·g(t); the velocity tiles of the copy equal h × velocity tiles of the original (lime).

atoms.idea: Page 418

pages.summary: Figure of a body frame moving relative to a fixed frame; body velocity g⁻¹ġ (left translation) and spatial velocity ġg⁻¹ (right translation); point velocity in terms of body coordinates.

atoms.label: Fig A.1
atoms.idea: Figure: body frame B moving along g_ab(t) relative to fixed frame A, carrying a point q from q(0) to q(t).
atoms.feynman: A sticker on a toy car rolling across a fixed floor grid.
atoms.visual: Slate frame A; blue body with frame B sliding/rotating along a path; a teal point q on it leaves a trail; scrub time.

atoms.idea: Left-translating with h = g⁻¹ gives the body velocity V̂^b = g⁻¹ġ, as in Chapter 2.
atoms.feynman: The car's speedometer and steering, felt from the driver's seat.
atoms.visual: Body view: the twist arrow drawn in B's frame (pink, rides along); 4×4 tiles of g⁻¹ġ.

atoms.idea: Right-translating gives the spatial velocity V̂^s = ġg⁻¹.
atoms.feynman: The same car's motion described by a camera fixed on the ceiling.
atoms.visual: Spatial view: the twist drawn at A's origin (gold, stays put) — it is the velocity of the imaginary body point passing through A's origin.

atoms.idea: For a body-fixed point, q_a(t) = g_ab(t) q_b, so v_a = ġ_ab q_b (A.6): ġ maps body coordinates of a point to its spatial velocity.
atoms.feynman: Where the sticker is on the car never changes; how fast it moves depends only on how the car moves.
atoms.visual: Teal point with fixed body coordinates; its velocity arrow computed as ġ·q_b updates as you move the point on the body.

atoms.idea: Page 419

pages.summary: Spatial and body velocities map point coordinates to velocities in one frame; they are related by Ad_g; forces are covectors whose translated versions are wrenches pairing with twists to give work.

atoms.idea: Continuation: ġ maps body point coordinates to spatial velocities.
atoms.feynman: The recipe from sticker position to sticker speed.
atoms.visual: Same teal point/arrow pair as before.

atoms.idea: To relate a point and its velocity in one frame: v_a = (ġg⁻¹) q_a, so the spatial velocity maps spatial coordinates to spatial velocity; similarly g⁻¹ġ maps body coordinates to body velocity.
atoms.feynman: Use one language for both "where" and "how fast", so you don't have to translate mid-sentence.
atoms.visual: Toggle "all in A" / "all in B": both the point and its arrow switch frames together, and the matrix used switches between V̂^s and V̂^b.

atoms.idea: Body and spatial velocities are the same instantaneous motion in two frames, related by V^s = Ad_g V^b.
atoms.feynman: The ceiling camera and the driver describe the same swerve with different numbers.
atoms.visual: Body twist (pink, at B) and spatial twist (gold, at A) with the 6×6 Ad tiles between them; a lime equality readout as you drag the body.

atoms.idea: A generalized force is a covector on SE(3); translating it to the dual Lie algebra (left = body frame, right = spatial frame) gives a wrench; its pairing with a twist is instantaneous work.
atoms.feynman: A push on a door: how much work it does depends on how the door moves, nothing more.
atoms.visual: Purple wrench (force arrow + torque curl) on the body, orange twist; a work meter shows ⟨F, V⟩ as a bar.

atoms.idea: Identifying se(3)* with R⁶, a wrench is F = (f, τ); the work is the R⁶ product F·V, but it is the natural covector–vector pairing, not an inner product.
atoms.feynman: A price list times a grocery list gives a bill, even though "price" and "apple" are different kinds of things.
atoms.visual: Six-slot bars for F (purple) and V (orange) side by side; matching slots multiply into a work total; a coral badge warns "not a ruler" if you try to measure F·F.

atoms.idea: Page 420

pages.summary: Wrench notation and same-frame pairing; transformation laws: spatial velocities change by Ad under change of inertial frame and are unaffected by change of body frame, and vice versa for body velocities.

atoms.idea: Wrenches are always written as R⁶ vectors with one subscript for their frame (F_a spatial, F_b body); work needs twist and wrench in the same frame: V^s_ab·F_a or V^b_ab·F_b.
atoms.feynman: You can only add up a bill when prices and quantities are in the same currency.
atoms.visual: Mismatch game: pair a body twist with a spatial wrench → coral wrong-work readout; switch both to the same frame → lime, and both choices give the same number.

atoms.idea: Subheading: transformation laws.
Changing the inertial frame from B to A: V^s_ac = Ad_{g_ab} V^s_bc, with the 6×6 matrix Ad_g = [[R, p̂R],[0, R]].
atoms.feynman: Re-describe a swerve from a different fixed camera: rotate the description, and the camera's offset adds extra apparent sideways speed.
atoms.visual: Two fixed cameras A and B; the spatial twist of C in each; the 6×6 Ad tiles (R blocks blue, p̂R block teal) transform one into the other live as you drag camera B.

atoms.idea: Changing to a new body frame rigidly attached (fixed g_bc) leaves the spatial velocity unchanged.
atoms.feynman: Moving the sticker you watch to another spot on the same car doesn't change how the ceiling camera describes the car's motion.
atoms.visual: Drag the body frame to a new spot on the body; the spatial twist readout stays frozen (lime).

atoms.idea: Body velocity is unaffected by changing the inertial frame, but changing the body frame transforms it by Ad_{g_bc⁻¹}.
atoms.feynman: The driver's feel doesn't care where the ceiling camera is, but a passenger seated elsewhere feels a different sideways sway.
atoms.visual: Drag camera A: body twist frozen (lime). Drag the body frame: body twist changes by Ad of the inverse offset (tiles light).

atoms.idea: Page 421

pages.summary: Velocities of chained motions add after Ad; wrenches transform by the transposed inverse adjoint; the R⁶ dot product of twists is not frame invariant.

atoms.idea: So Ad expresses a change of body frame on body velocities.
atoms.feynman: Re-seating the passenger changes their felt sway by a fixed rule.
atoms.visual: Same Ad tiles as before.

atoms.idea: When both g_ab(t) and g_bc(t) move, velocities add only in a common frame: V^s_ac = V^s_ab + Ad_{g_ab} V^s_bc.
atoms.feynman: Walking on a moving train: your speed relative to the ground is the train's speed plus your walking speed turned into ground directions.
atoms.visual: Two-link chain A→B→C both moving; orange V_ab and blue V_bc (re-expressed by Ad into A) add tip-to-tail into the pink V_ac.

atoms.idea: Wrenches change fixed frames by the coadjoint rule F_b = Ad_{g_ab⁻¹}ᵀ F_a.
atoms.feynman: Re-label the price list the opposite way to the goods, so the bill stays right.
atoms.visual: Purple wrench in frame A and frame B; Ad-inverse-transpose tiles between them; work with a twist stays frozen.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.3.2: metric properties of SE(3).
The R⁶ dot product on twists is not frame invariant: ξ₁′·ξ₂′ = ξ₁ᵀ Ad_gᵀAd_g ξ₂ ≠ ξ₁·ξ₂ when p ≠ 0, so orthogonal twists can stop being orthogonal.
atoms.feynman: Two hallways that meet at a right angle on one floor plan look skewed in a plan drawn from another corner — if your ruler secretly mixes turning with sliding.
atoms.visual: Two twists with a lime right-angle badge; drag the frame origin p; the dot-product readout drifts from 0 and the badge turns coral; at p=0 (pure rotation of frame) it stays lime.

atoms.idea: Misusing the R⁶ inner product caused confusion in the literature; the section shows no frame-invariant inner product on se(3) exists.
atoms.feynman: People argued about distances measured with a ruler that changes when you walk around it.
atoms.visual: A short "myth" card stack: the R⁶ ruler stamped coral, flipping to the next beats.

atoms.idea: Page 422

pages.summary: Metrics and pseudo-metrics on Rⁿ; invariance under rotations forces commuting with all rotations; Lemma A.2: then the metric is a multiple of the identity.

atoms.idea: Continuation: no invariant inner product on se(3), and its consequences.
atoms.feynman: The ruler question will be settled.
atoms.visual: Card stack continues.

atoms.idea: Subheading: invariant metrics on Rⁿ.
A metric Ψ on Rⁿ is a symmetric, positive-definite bilinear form; in an orthonormal basis it is a matrix with Ψ(v,w) = vᵀΨw.
atoms.feynman: A ruler that might be stretchy in some directions but never gives a negative or zero length to a real arrow.
atoms.visual: Ruler-ellipse: the unit ball of Ψ drawn as an ellipse; drag its axes; lengths of an orange arrow read off by Ψ.

atoms.idea: Positive definite implies invertible; a symmetric nondegenerate form that may be indefinite is a pseudo-metric.
atoms.feynman: A "ruler" that can give some arrows negative length, but never ignores an arrow completely.
atoms.visual: Ellipse morphs into a hyperbola (pseudo-metric, purple) when one eigenvalue slider crosses zero; at exactly zero it collapses to parallel lines (degenerate, coral).

atoms.label: Eqs (A.7)–(A.9)
atoms.idea: Vectors change frames by v_a = R v_b; a metric is frame-invariant if Ψ(Rv₁, Rv₂) = Ψ(v₁,v₂) for all rotations, i.e. ΨR = RΨ.
atoms.feynman: A ruler is fair if turning your head doesn't change the lengths you measure.
atoms.visual: Spin the frame with a rotation knob; the ruler-ellipse is redrawn in the new frame; a mismatch meter compares lengths before/after.

atoms.label: Lemma A.2
atoms.idea: A symmetric matrix commuting with every rotation is a multiple of the identity.
atoms.feynman: The only shape that looks the same no matter how you turn it is a perfect circle.
atoms.visual: Try ellipses: spinning a non-circular one makes the mismatch meter flash coral; only when both axes are equal does it stay lime for all spins.

atoms.idea: Page 423

pages.summary: Proof of Lemma A.2; invariant metric on Rⁿ is unique up to length scale; metrics and pull backs on manifolds; left, right and bi-invariant metrics via conjugation.

atoms.idea: Proof: if v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ, then Rv is too for every rotation, so every unit vector is an eigenvector with λ, hence Ψ = λI.
atoms.feynman: If one direction is "long", turning it shows every direction must be equally long.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) one eigen-arrow with its stretch λ; (2) rotate it — the arrow still stretches by λ; (3) sweep all rotations: arrows cover the circle, all stretched equally → circle.

atoms.idea: The scalar α picks a unit of length (meters, feet); with it fixed, the invariant metric on R³ is unique.
atoms.feynman: The circle's size just says whether you measure in centimeters or inches.
atoms.visual: A unit slider rescales the circle; the lime "invariant" badge stays on for every size.

atoms.label: Prop A.3
atoms.idea: Up to scale, Rⁿ has exactly one frame-invariant positive-definite metric.
atoms.feynman: Every fair ruler in flat space is the ordinary ruler with some unit.
atoms.visual: Summary card: a single circle with a scale knob, lime crown.

atoms.idea: Subheading: invariant metrics on SE(3).
Does SE(3) have a frame-invariant metric, giving twists a fair "speed"? Since SE(3) is a manifold, metrics must be defined on tangent spaces.
atoms.feynman: Can we build a fair speedometer for a tumbling, sliding box?
atoms.visual: A box both spinning and sliding with a blank speedometer dial; a question-mark wobble.

atoms.idea: A quadratic form on M is a smoothly varying symmetric bilinear form on each tangent space (metric if positive definite, pseudo-metric if nondegenerate); its pull back by F is F^*Ψ(v,w) = Ψ(TF v, TF w); Ψ is F-invariant if F^*Ψ = Ψ.
atoms.feynman: A ruler glued at every spot of a curved world, and a map is fair if it never changes what the rulers read.
atoms.visual: Small ruler-ellipses drawn on tangent sheets across a surface; apply a map F: the pulled-back ellipses either coincide with the originals (lime) or not (coral).

atoms.idea: Define a metric at e and spread it by left (or right) translation to get a left (right) invariant metric; bi-invariant means both, equivalently invariant under every conjugation I_h(g) = hgh⁻¹.
atoms.feynman: Copy one ruler everywhere by walking in body directions, or by world directions; a perfect ruler would agree either way.
atoms.visual: Home ellipse copied by L_g (orange copies) and by R_g (blue copies); where they disagree, coral; bi-invariant would make all copies overlap.

atoms.idea: Page 424

pages.summary: Lemma A.4 reduces bi-invariance to Ad-invariance at the identity; Proposition A.5 characterizes bi-invariant forms; first proof step sets up the block equation.

atoms.idea: The same definitions apply to indefinite quadratic forms.
atoms.feynman: The rules hold for funny rulers too.
atoms.visual: Hyperbola-shaped rulers also allowed in the panel (purple).

atoms.label: Lemma A.4
atoms.idea: A left- (or right-) invariant form is conjugation-invariant iff at the identity Ψ_e(Ad_h ξ, Ad_h η) = Ψ_e(ξ, η) for all h.
atoms.feynman: To check fairness everywhere, it's enough to check at home that re-describing from any viewpoint keeps the reading.
atoms.visual: Home tangent sheet with two twists; random h buttons apply Ad_h to both; a Ψ readout must stay constant (lime) for the form to pass.

atoms.idea: Proof: necessity is immediate; for sufficiency, write T_eI_h via L_h and R_{h⁻¹}, use Ad-invariance at e and left invariance to show right invariance, hence bi-invariance.
atoms.feynman: If the ruler is fair at home and copies fairly by walking, then it also copies fairly by world moves.
atoms.visual: Staircase of four frames: (1) Ad-invariant at e; (2) split conjugation into a left and a right move; (3) cancel the left move by left invariance; (4) what remains is right invariance (lime).

atoms.label: Prop A.5
atoms.idea: A left-invariant form on SE(3) is bi-invariant iff, at e (with se(3) ≅ R⁶ as (v,ω)), its matrix is [[0, βI],[βI, γI]].
atoms.feynman: The only fair "speed scores" for a tumbling box ignore pure sliding on its own and only see sliding-times-spinning and spinning-times-spinning.
atoms.visual: A 6×6 tile grid in four 3×3 blocks; only the off-diagonal β blocks and the lower γ block may light; the upper-left block is pinned dark.

atoms.idea: Proof step 1: by Lemma A.4, bi-invariance means AdᵀΨ_eAd = Ψ_e for all h (A.10–A.11), with Ψ_e = [[A, B],[Bᵀ, C]].
atoms.feynman: Write the unknown ruler as four tiles and demand that every viewpoint change leaves the tiles the same.
atoms.visual: A random-h shaker applies AdᵀΨAd to a user-filled 6×6 grid; tiles that change flash coral.

atoms.idea: Page 425

pages.summary: Proof of Prop A.5 via block equations and Lemma A.2; the hyperbolic metric (reciprocal product) as a pseudo-metric depending on length scale.

atoms.idea: Proof step 2: expanding with Ad_h = [[R, p̂R],[0, R]] gives three block equations (A.12) for A, B, C.
atoms.feynman: Spell out what each tile must satisfy.
atoms.visual: The three block equations appear as three rows of tile pictures, each tile colored by which of A, B, C feeds it.

atoms.idea: Proof step 3: Lemma A.2 makes A = αI; setting p = 0 makes B = βI, C = γI; then the p-dependent terms force α = 0.
atoms.feynman: Rotations make each tile round; then sliding the viewpoint shows the slide-slide tile must be empty.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) spin-only shaker: tiles become multiples of I; (2) add slide p: the A tile leaks into the C tile through p̂ (coral) unless α = 0; (3) α slider snaps to 0, everything lime.

atoms.idea: Two special bi-invariant forms follow.
atoms.feynman: Two famous fair-ish speed scores.
atoms.visual: β, γ plane with two marked points: (1,0) and (0,−4).

atoms.label: Ex A.21, Eq (A.13)
atoms.idea: The hyperbolic metric (β=1, γ=0): ⟨(v₁,ω₁),(v₂,ω₂)⟩_H = v₁ᵀω₂ + v₂ᵀω₁; eigenvalues ±1 in pairs, so some twists have negative "length".
atoms.feynman: A score that multiplies sliding by spinning: a twist that slides one way while spinning the other scores negative, like a left-handed vs right-handed screw.
atoms.visual: Screw with pitch slider; H-score readout = 2·(v·ω) changes sign as pitch passes 0 (right-handed lime, left-handed coral); eigenvalue bars ±1.

atoms.idea: The hyperbolic form depends on length scale (fixes the ratio of unit slide to unit turn); it is nondegenerate, so a pseudo-metric; it equals the reciprocal product of Chapter 2 and is a case of the Klein form [13].
atoms.feynman: Changing from meters to millimeters multiplies the score by 1000, though signs and zeros stay.
atoms.visual: Unit slider rescales the H-readout linearly; zero crossings stay at the same pitch.

atoms.idea: Page 426

pages.summary: The Killing form is degenerate and scale-free; no bi-invariant positive-definite metric exists on SE(3); left-invariant metrics depend on frame origin and length scale; twist magnitude and pitch are invariants.

atoms.label: Ex A.22, Eq (A.14)
atoms.idea: The Killing form (β=0, γ=−4): ⟨ξ₁,ξ₂⟩_K = −4ω₁ᵀω₂; degenerate (ignores translation), so neither metric nor pseudo-metric, and independent of length scale.
atoms.feynman: A score that only counts spinning and is blind to sliding.
atoms.visual: K-readout bar: pure-slide twists read 0 (coral "blind" eye icon); scaling units leaves the bar unchanged.

atoms.idea: The general Killing form is trace(ad_ξ₁ ad_ξ₂) with ad_ξ(η) = [ξ, η]; the −4 matches this definition.
atoms.feynman: Measure a twist by how strongly its bracket stirs up all other twists.
atoms.visual: 6×6 ad-matrices of two twists multiply; their trace tile sum equals −4ω₁·ω₂ readout (lime).

atoms.label: Cor A.5.1
atoms.idea: Every bi-invariant form gives pure translations zero length, so no bi-invariant positive-definite metric exists on SE(3).
atoms.feynman: There is no fair speedometer for a box that both spins and slides: any fair one goes blind to sliding.
atoms.visual: Set ω=0 and slide: every bi-invariant (β, γ) choice reads 0 → coral 🚫 over the "metric" crown.

atoms.idea: Lengths on SE(3) are still possible but require a choice; restricting to left (or right) invariant metrics gives the next result.
atoms.feynman: You can still build a speedometer; you just have to decide where your "center" is and how to trade meters for radians.
atoms.visual: Two dials appear: frame-origin picker and meters-per-radian knob.

atoms.label: Prop A.6
atoms.idea: Left- (right-) invariant metrics on SE(3) are parameterized by a choice of reference-frame origin and length scale [63].
atoms.feynman: A speedometer for a tumbling box is fixed once you pick the reference point and how many meters equal one radian.
atoms.visual: Move the origin dot and turn the scale knob: the twist-length readouts of a fixed motion change; with both fixed, readouts become stable.

atoms.idea: Examples show the consequences for kinematics and control.
atoms.feynman: Now see why this matters for real robots.
atoms.visual: Panel tabs: twists, constraints, manipulability.

atoms.label: Ex A.23
atoms.idea: For twists with ω ≠ 0 (proper screws), magnitude and pitch can be rewritten via the Killing and hyperbolic forms.
atoms.feynman: Two facts about a screw — how hard it spins and how far it advances per turn — can be read with fair tools.
atoms.visual: Gold screw with M and h dials; the dials are computed from K and H readouts.

atoms.idea: Page 427

pages.summary: Magnitude and pitch as invariant ratios; constraints on SE(3) give covectors pulled back to se(3)*: constraint forces and free motions annihilate regardless of frame; treating constraints as twists is a mistake.

atoms.idea: M = −¼⟨ξ,ξ⟩_K and h = −2⟨ξ,ξ⟩_H/⟨ξ,ξ⟩_K, so both are frame-independent for screws with nonzero rotation.
atoms.feynman: A bolt's turn rate and thread pitch don't depend on where you stand.
atoms.visual: Drag the reference frame anywhere: twist coordinates change wildly, but M and h dials stay frozen (lime).

atoms.idea: Pitch depends on the length scale (a ratio of translation to rotation), matching the scale choice needed by the hyperbolic metric.
atoms.feynman: Thread pitch in millimeters per turn becomes a different number in inches per turn.
atoms.visual: Unit knob rescales only the h dial; M stays put.

atoms.label: Ex A.24, Eq (A.15)
atoms.idea: Hybrid force control: contact constraints fᵢ(g) = 0 differentiate to ⟨dfᵢ(g), ġ⟩ = 0; translating to the identity gives ⟨L_g^* dfᵢ, ξ⟩ = 0 with ξ = g⁻¹ġ and L_g^*dfᵢ ∈ se(3)*.
atoms.feynman: A hand sliding on a tabletop: its allowed motions are "anything that doesn't push into the table".
atoms.visual: Pink tool tip on a slate table; constraint covector shown as a purple stack of planes parallel to the table; any orange twist crossing zero planes is allowed (lime), others coral.

atoms.idea: These covectors span the constraint forces; their annihilator in se(3) is the space of free motions; the two annihilate (zero work) in every frame, though each subspace's coordinates change.
atoms.feynman: The table pushes straight up; you slide sideways; the push does no work on the slide, from anyone's viewpoint.
atoms.visual: Purple constraint wrenches and lime free twists; a work meter reads 0 for every pair; dragging the frame origin changes all numbers but the meter stays 0.

atoms.idea: A common mistake treats constraint directions as twists and uses the R⁶ dot product to decide orthogonality to free motions.
atoms.feynman: Using a crooked ruler to decide which pushes are "perpendicular" to sliding.
atoms.visual: Toggle "mistake mode": constraints drawn as orange twists with right-angle badges based on R⁶ dot product.

atoms.idea: Page 428

pages.summary: Twist-based constraint descriptions break under frame change; the covector description is invariant; left-invariant constraints are subgroups (Loncaric); manipulability measures based on R⁶ norms need care.

atoms.idea: That twist-based description is not frame invariant because SE(3) has no invariant metric, hence no invariant orthogonality.
atoms.feynman: The crooked ruler gives different answers from different seats.
atoms.visual: In mistake mode, drag the frame origin: the right-angle badges flip coral although the physical contact is unchanged.

atoms.idea: Fix: constraints are covectors; under a frame change V′ = Ad_g V and F′ = Ad_{g⁻¹}ᵀ F, so F′·V′ = F·V; the pairing also scales correctly with units.
atoms.feynman: Pushes and motions change in opposite ways when you switch viewpoint, so the work they share never changes.
atoms.visual: Correct mode: twists transform by Ad tiles, wrenches by inverse-transpose tiles; the work readout stays exactly 0 for every frame and every unit choice (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.25
atoms.idea: Constraint covectors pulled to se(3)* can vary with g; a constraint is left invariant if L_g^*df(g) = df(e), i.e. free directions are constant in the body frame — e.g. sliding on a flat surface.
atoms.feynman: An ice skater on a flat rink: whichever way she faces, "forward-sideways-and-spin" are always allowed, measured from her own body.
atoms.visual: Puck on a flat slate plane: body-frame free directions (lime arrows) stay constant as it moves; on a bumpy surface they tilt with g (coral).

atoms.label: Prop A.7
atoms.idea: A constraint f(g) = 0 is left (or right) invariant iff its zero set is a subgroup of SE(3) [63].
atoms.feynman: The moves that keep a puck on a flat table can be combined and undone and still keep it on the table: they form their own club.
atoms.visual: Compose two allowed puck motions (lime) → result is allowed; on a curved bowl the composition leaves the surface (coral).

atoms.label: Ex A.26
atoms.idea: Manipulability measures from Chapter 3 that use the Euclidean metric on R⁶ ≅ se(3) are not frame invariant, so use them with care.
atoms.feynman: Grading how nimble a hand is with a crooked ruler gives grades that depend on where you put the measuring tape.
atoms.visual: Arm with its twist manipulability ellipsoid; a "tool frame" handle on the end-effector.

atoms.idea: Page 429

pages.summary: Two tool frames give Jacobians related by Ad, so σmin and condition number depend on frame choice; volume forms and the determinant.

atoms.label: Ex A.26
atoms.idea: With tool frames T1, T2, J₁ = Ad_h J₂; Ad_h does not preserve the R⁶ norm, so σmin(J₁) ≠ σmin(J₂) and even its maximizing posture differs: maximizing σmin (or condition number) is ill-posed.
atoms.feynman: Judging a hand's weakest direction depends on whether you hold the ruler at the wrist or at the fingertip.
atoms.visual: Same 6-DOF arm, two tool-frame handles; side-by-side σmin bars and condition-number bars differ; scanning a joint slider, the best posture marker (gold) sits at different angles for T1 and T2.

atoms.idea: Subsection A.3.3: volume forms on SE(3).
Since lengths need choices, how much does volume on SE(3) depend on frame and scale? This matters for measuring workspace size [9].
atoms.feynman: Even if we can't agree on a ruler, can we agree on how big a closet is?
atoms.visual: A robot's reachable cloud of poses glows; a volume meter with a question mark.

atoms.idea: A volume form is a nowhere-zero skew multilinear map of n tangent vectors; it gives the volume of their parallelepiped and integrates to volumes; on Rⁿ it is det[V₁ … Vₙ].
atoms.feynman: The space inside a box built from three sticks: swap two sticks and it flips sign; squash them flat and it's zero.
atoms.visual: Three orange arrows span a blue box; gold volume readout = det; swapping two arrows flips the sign (handedness color flip); dragging one into the plane of the others → 0.

atoms.idea: Page 430

pages.summary: Pulled-back volume forms scale by det J; Theorem A.8: left-invariant volume forms on SE(3) are bi-invariant because det Ad = 1; a product volume form using the triple product on so(3) gives SO(3) volume 8π³.

atoms.label: Eq (A.16)
atoms.idea: Pulling back a volume form by F multiplies it by det J (change of variables); left, right, bi-invariant volume forms are defined as for metrics.
atoms.feynman: Squeeze a sponge: every small cube's volume changes by the same squeeze factor at that spot.
atoms.visual: A grid of tiny boxes deformed by a map F; each box's volume ratio colored; readout equals det J at that point.

atoms.label: Thm A.8
atoms.idea: Every left-invariant volume form on SE(3) is also right invariant, hence bi-invariant.
atoms.feynman: Even though no ruler is fair, every fair-by-walking measuring cup is fair from every viewpoint.
atoms.visual: 6D box meter: apply random left moves and conjugations; the volume readout stays at exactly 1× (lime crown).

atoms.idea: Sketch: it suffices that det(T_eI_h) = 1; the Jacobian of conjugation at e is Ad_h, and det [[R, p̂R],[0, R]] = det R · det R = 1.
atoms.feynman: The viewpoint change may shear the box but never grows or shrinks it — like sliding a deck of cards sideways.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) conjugation's Jacobian = Ad tiles; (2) block-triangular → det = det R × det R; (3) each = 1; (4) the 6D box shears (teal) but its volume bar stays 1.

atoms.idea: So SE(3) has a bi-invariant volume form, e.g. standard volume on R³ times a volume on so(3) given by −¼⟨ω₁,[ω₂,ω₃]⟩_K = ω₁·(ω₂×ω₃) (the triple product); with it SO(3) has volume 8π³.
atoms.feynman: Measure a closet of poses as "how much space to stand in" times "how many ways to face"; facing-space totals 8π³.
atoms.visual: SO(3) as a ball of rotation vectors of radius π; a fill animation counts volume; triple-product box of three ω arrows; final readout 8π³ ≈ 248 (with the antipodal-identification shell explained by a coral shimmer).

atoms.idea: This product volume form depends on the length scale (continued).
atoms.feynman: Change meters to centimeters and the standing-space part grows.
atoms.visual: Unit knob rescales the R³ factor of the volume meter.

atoms.idea: Page 431

pages.summary: Volume trades translation vs rotation through the length scale but comparisons are scale-free; det J manipulability is frame-independent; manipulator length and a work-volume bound for 6R arms.

atoms.idea: The scale sets the trade-off between translational and angular volume; once fixed, volume is frame-independent, and since scale changes multiply all volumes equally, "which is bigger" is scale-free.
atoms.feynman: Measuring two closets in inches or centimeters gives different numbers but the same winner.
atoms.visual: Two workspace clouds with volume bars; turn the unit knob: both bars scale together and the gold "bigger" crown never moves.

atoms.label: Ex A.27
atoms.idea: det J manipulability uses the standard R⁶ volume; it is frame-independent since det(Ad_h J₂) = det Ad_h · det J₂ = det J₂.
atoms.feynman: The ruler was crooked, but the measuring cup is honest: the hand's "volume of nimbleness" is the same from any tool frame.
atoms.visual: Same two-tool-frame arm from the metric scene: σmin bars disagree (coral) while det J bars agree exactly (lime).

atoms.label: Ex A.28
atoms.idea: Optimal 6R design [85, 86]: with POE kinematics, the manipulator length L_M is the shortest total length of a chain of segments linking the six joint axes; it does not depend on the reference configuration (an exercise).
atoms.feynman: The shortest string you could tie between six rods hung in the air.
atoms.visual: Six gold joint-axis lines in 3D; a teal string with beads sliding on each axis; drag beads and watch the total length bar; an "optimize" button shrinks it to L_M.

atoms.idea: Work volume V_M = ∫ over g(Q) of a bi-invariant volume form (Q = 6-torus of joints); with the product form, V_M ≤ (4/3)π L_M³ · 8π³.
atoms.feynman: The most closet space an arm of total length L can cover is a full ball of radius L, with every facing direction at every point.
atoms.visual: Monte-Carlo fill: sampled joint angles map to poses that splat into a position cloud colored by orientation coverage; a bar fills toward the bound (4/3)πL³·8π³.

atoms.idea: Page 432

pages.summary: Figure of an elbow manipulator; the volume bound is frame-free; elbow and inverse-elbow arms; Theorem A.9: maximal work volume iff elbow (or inverse) with elbow at the midpoint.

atoms.label: Fig A.2
atoms.idea: Figure: an elbow manipulator — two-axis shoulder, elbow, and three-axis wrist with intersecting orthogonal axes, link lengths l₀, l₁, l₂.
atoms.feynman: A human arm: shoulder that swings two ways, an elbow hinge, and a wrist that can point any way.
atoms.visual: 3D elbow arm: six orange joint cylinders labelled only by axis arrows; shoulder axes meet at q₁ and the three wrist axes meet at one point (gold dot).

atoms.idea: A 6R arm achieving the bound has maximal work volume; the bound is independent of base/tool frames but depends on scale, which doesn't affect comparisons — so it defines an optimal manipulator.
atoms.feynman: A fair contest: arms of the same total length compete for the most closet space.
atoms.visual: Leaderboard of arm designs with work-volume bars normalized by the bound.

atoms.idea: An elbow manipulator has a shoulder and wrist each with mutually orthogonal intersecting axes, plus an elbow; its inverse swaps wrist and shoulder.
atoms.feynman: Your arm, or your arm flipped so the wrist is at the shoulder.
atoms.visual: Toggle between elbow arm and its inverse (wrist at the base); both drawn in orange/pink.

atoms.label: Thm A.9
atoms.idea: A 6R arm of given length has maximal work volume iff it is an elbow manipulator (or its inverse) with the elbow midway between shoulder and wrist [85, 86].
atoms.feynman: The best arm is like yours, with upper arm and forearm the same length.
atoms.visual: Elbow-position slider along the arm: work-volume bar peaks exactly at the midpoint (gold crown); off-center, a coral hole opens in the middle of the position cloud.

atoms.idea: Why: the end wrist reaches every orientation everywhere, and the midway elbow leaves no hole at the workspace center.
atoms.feynman: With equal upper and forearm you can touch your own shoulder; with a short forearm you can't reach close in.
atoms.visual: Cross-section of the reachable disc for unequal links shows an empty coral inner ring; equal links fill to the center (lime).
